Random Kitchen Sinks
Roger. I will summarize the meaning and implementation intuition of "approximation (random features x linear regression)" in the following order: intuition, equation, procedure, and hook-up point.
Approximate what?
The original GP (Gaussian process regression) uses the kernel (k(x,x')) to express smoothness, where close points are close predictions.
However, strictly speaking GP is O(N³) (N=number of study points) and heavy.

Then, we create an explicit feature map (\phi(x)) that is "kernel ≈ inner product" with random features ([Random Fourier Features]; [RFF]), and perform [linear regression] (≈[Bayesian linear regression]) on it.
This is GP approximation by "random features x linear regression".
Also known as Random Kitchen Sinks.
Intuition (why does it work?)
[RBF] system kernel can be expressed by Fourier transform → Adding random waves (frequency and phase) approximates a "smooth" function space.
So if we convert "φ(x) = vector of random waves" and learn (\hat y = w^\top \phi(x)), we can replace nonlinear regression with linear regression.
Formula (minimum set)
1) Random features (example of RBF kernel)
Random (\omega_j \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{\ell^2}I)), (b_j \sim \mathrm{Unif}[0,2\pi])
Feature mapping (dimension D)
\phi_j(x) = \sqrt{\frac{2}{D}} \cos(\omega_j^\top x + b_j), \quad j=1,\dots,D
Then (k(x,x')\approx \phi(x)^\top \phi(x'))
If the embedding is **normalized (L2=1)**, then instead of Euclidean distance
The RBF equivalent using the cosine distance (1 - x\cdot x') is also acceptable in practice.
It is sufficient to simply follow the "random projection -> cos" for implementation.
2) Linear regression (Bayesian version = can also produce uncertainty)
Observation: (y = \Phi w + \varepsilon), (\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_n^2 I))
where (\Phi) is ([ \phi(x_1)^\top; \dots; \phi(x_N)^\top ])
Pre: (w \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\lambda^{-1} I)) (ridge regularization)
Posterior mean and variance:
\Sigma = \big(\lambda I + \tfrac{1}{\sigma_n^2}\Phi^\top \Phi \big)^{-1},\qquad
\mu_w = \tfrac{1}{\sigma_n^2}\Sigma, \Phi^\top y
Predicted mean and variance (new point (x_)):
\mu(x_) = \phi(x_)^\top \mu_w,\quad
\mathrm{Var}(x_) \approx \phi(x_)^\top \Sigma, \phi(x_) + \sigma_n^2
UCB is (\text{UCB}(x)=\mu(x)+\sqrt{\beta},\sigma(x))
So far, **GP-like "average + uncertainty "** can be obtained at a low cost.
Procedure (Implementation Flow)
1. pre-processing
Text -> Embedded (e.g., 1536 dimensions)
L2 normalization (important: easy to use cosine for distance)
2. preparation of RFF (one time only)
Determine dimension D (256 to 1024 for MVP)
Fixed random numbers (\omega, b) (seed retained/not regenerated each time)
3. study set creation
Create (\Phi) from the evaluated ((x_i, y_i))
Compute (\Sigma, \mu_w) (D×D matrix inverted once)
4. inference of unrated points
Apply φ(x) to each (x) to obtain (\mu(x), \sigma(x))
Arranged in UCB order and presented in MMR to ensure diversity
5. re-study (light) when new evaluations are accumulated
Parameter Guideline
D (RFF dimension): 256 (ultralight) to 1024 (accuracy up, cost up)
(\ell) (length scale): 0.5 to 1.0 equivalent (depends on the distance of embedding)
(\lambda) (prior accuracy, ridge): from around 1.0. Raise by over-learning.
(\sigma_n) (Observation noise): around 0.2 (Measures for blurring of evaluation. Can be estimated from duplicate evaluations)
(\beta) (search degree of UCB): 1.0 to 2.0 (the larger the value, the closer to search)
What is "light" about it?
The bottleneck is the inverse (once) of D×D, O(D³).
If D=512, even JS/Deno can fit in a few hundred ms to a few seconds.
Subsequent inferences are made at each point O(D) (fast).
It is much lighter than O(N³) in strict GP.
Common Pitfalls
RFF is regenerated every time → φ does not match between learning and inference and collapses.
→ Random numbers are fixed (seed management).
Embedding is not normalized → distance scale is broken and σ is strange.
→ Ensure that L2=1.
D is too small → Bias (lack of expression).
→ Verified by increasing from 256 to 512 to 1024....
Numerical instability → (\lambda) slightly higher / double precision / small epsilon to prevent divergence.
UCBs are all similar candidates → diversity penalty in MMR (deduct the cosine maximum with the already selected).
Minimal pseudo code (TypeScript/Edge Functions style)
code:ts
// Preparation (1 time): RFF parameters
const D = 512, l = 0.7; // dimension and length scales
const W = randn(d, D, 1/(l*l));    // N(0, 1/l^2)
const b = uniform(D, 0, 2*Math.PI);
const phi = (x: number[]) => {
const u = l2norm1(x); // L2 normalization
const z = new Array(D);
for (let j=0;j<D;j++){
let s = 0; for (let i=0;i<d;i++) s += W[i][j]*u[i];
z[j] = Math.SQRT2*Math.cos(s + b[j])/Math.sqrt(D);
return z;
// Learning (each time an evaluation is accumulated)
const Phi = X_labeled.map(phi);    // N×D
const XtX = gram(Phi);             // D×D
const A   = addDiag(XtX, lambda);  // ridge
const Ainv= inv(A);
const Xty = Phi[0].map((_,j)=> dotCol(Phi,j, y)); // D×1
const w   = matvec(Ainv, Xty);
// Prediction (not yet evaluated)
for (const x of X_unlabeled) {
const p  = phi(x);
const mu = dot(w, p);
const var= quad(p, Ainv) + sigma_n*sigma_n;
const ucb= mu + Math.sqrt(beta)*Math.sqrt(var);
// → ucb order + presented in MMR
summary
RFF x linear regression is a lightweight practical approximation to the "mean and uncertainty" of GP.
Ideal for low-cost MVP as it also turns in Edge Functions (Deno/TS).
First, D=256-512, L2 normalization, fixed random numbers, UCB coefficient=1.5 is sufficient.
If it is not enough, move to D↑ or **Python worker (GPyTorch)**.

pages.title: The political ideology of conversational AI: Converging evidence on ChatGPT's pro-environmental, left-libertarian orientation

lines.text: The political ideology of conversational AI: Converging evidence on ChatGPT's pro-environmental, left-libertarian orientation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.01768
[The political ideology of conversational AI]
[pro-environmental], [left-libertarian]
[GPT5.icon]
What did the paper show?
An early audit study that asked ChatGPT for a large number of responses to political claims and demonstrated an environmental focus and left-libertarian leaning.
Design (rough)

630 political statements derived from the Voting Assistance Tool + Political Compass claims were used and evaluated in three **pre-registered** experiments. Robustness checks were also conducted, such as using negative form, reversing the order of presentation, changing the formality of the style, and using multiple languages (English, German, Dutch, and Spanish).
Specific examples of main results

ChatGPT showed a tendency to respond in favor of taxing airplanes/supporting controlling rent increases/supporting legalizing abortion, and was estimated to vote for the Green Party (Bündnis 90/Die Grünen/GroenLinks) in the German and Dutch general elections in 2021.
implication

Suggests that dialogue AI used for information retrieval and decision support may return politically nuanced summaries and advice. In addition to model selection and prompt design, bias mitigation designs such as multiple model use, mirror prompts (positive/negative pair presentation), order randomization, and human review will be necessary.
notes

The target is the initial ChatGPT, and the behavior can change with learning and policy updates. In addition, note that the conclusions will be swayed by the design of the evaluation axis, as it depends on VAA (voting assistance)-derived questions.

pages.title: A Systematic Survey of Automatic Prompt Optimization Techniques

lines.text: A Systematic Survey of Automatic Prompt Optimization Techniques
2025 https://arxiv.org/pdf/2502.16923
[GPT5.icon]
1 piece summary
Theme: "[Automatic Prompt Optimization] ([APO])" = a survey of black box optimization that does not touch the weights of the model, only the prompts to improve performance automatically.

CORE: A five-part framework of "1) seed creation → 2) evaluation and feedback → 3) candidate generation → 4) selection and exploration → 5) iteration" that comprehensively categorizes existing research.

Benefits: rule editing, evolutionary computation, RL, LLM evaluation, metaprompts, MoE, program synthesis (DSPY system), etc. are made into components and assembled according to task characteristics and cost.
Caveats: dev overlearning, evaluator (LLM-as-a-judge) bias, Gibbs-Rich splitter/"evil twin" phenomenon, failure to self-reflect, cost explosion.
Key Points of the 5-Part Framework
1. seed prompts
Handwriting (ProteGi, SPRIG, etc.)
Induction by LLM = Instruction Induction (APE, DAPO, MOP); also README and structured temp filling groups (SCULPT, UniPrompt).
Inference Evaluation & Feedback
Numerical evaluation: task correctness/execution accuracy, BLEU/ROUGE/BERTScore, reward model, (log probability required) NLL/entropy.
LLM Feedback: polish 1 candidate (SCULPT, PACE, CRISPO) / improve multiple candidates at once (ProTeGi, PromptAgent, PREFER, SOS).
People feedback: GATE, PROMST, APOHF, etc.
Candidate Generation
Heuristic Editing:.
Monte Carlo/MCTS (ProTeGi, PromptAgent)
Genetic Algo (SPRIG, PromptBreeder, EvoPrompt, StraGo)
Word/phrase level substitution and lexical pruning (COPLE, CLAPS, BDPL, PIN)
Editing with auxiliary NN: RL (RLPrompt, OIRL, PRewrite), small LLM fine-tuning (BPO, FIPO), GAN-like framework.
Meta-prompt design ([OPRO], PE2, DAPO)
Coverage oriented:.
Branch extension of single prompt (AMPO)
Mixture-of-Experts (MOP: Prompt by Cluster)
Ensemble (PromptBoosting, PREFER, GPO)
Program synthesis: DSP/[DSPY], MIPRO, SAMMO... Optimized instructions and examples by module.
4. search & select
Top-K Greed, UCB/UCT (Bandit) (ProTeGi, PromptAgent, SPRIG, AELP),
Simultaneous domain-specific search (RBJS: MOP), meta-heuristics mixed (PLUM).
Iteration Depth (repetition)
Fixed number of times OR early termination (negative gain continues/threshold reached).
Representative Methodology "Positioning One Word Memo
OPRO: Linguistically optimize "better directives" with "metaprompts". Generic and easy to implement.
ProTeGi / PromptAgent: LLM feedback + MCTS/UCB to turn discrete search in a solid way.
APE: Instruction Induction classic. A strong foundation for initial prompt creation.
SPRIG: System prompt optimization is also a shot in the arm. Large scale but works.
CRISPO: Critique from multiple perspectives (accuracy/style/integrity...) → revision. Effective for generative systems.
MOP: MoE-like cluster-specific prompts to select the best expert for each input.
DSPY/MIPRO/SAMMO: "Design studies" to train each stage of the LLM pipeline in parts simultaneously.
AMPO: Absorb failure patterns with branching and ensure coverage with if-then branches.
COPLE: Shows that synonymous substitution of influence words alone works great. Also good for post-processing optimization.
Usage Guide (practical tips)
Classification/MCQ-centered/small amount of data: ProTeGi system with Top-K + UCB; easy to apply COPLE word substitution at the end.
Summary/translation/creation and other generative systems: LLM critique -> revision (CRISPO/PE2) + small amount of human FB for high return.
Domain wide/input diverse: Robust with MOP (MoE) and ensemble.
Long procedure instructions required: SCULPT (hierarchical and polished), AMPO (branching to seal omissions).
Multi-stage RAG/tool linkage: Optimize instructions and examples per stage with DSPY/MIPRO.
Security/safety is also simultaneously optimal: SOS (performance x safety multi-purpose optimal).
Anyway, low-cost initial line: random delimiters and simple revisions are surprisingly strong (strong baseline).
Mini Blueprint for Experimental Design
D_val: 50-200 cases (diversity oriented). k=8-16 candidates, N=5-15 iterations.
Evaluation: log primary goal (percentage correct/accuracy of execution) + sub-goals (safety/appearance/length) with multiple objectives.
Search: Top-K -> UCB (or UCT). Improvement < epsilon p consecutive early stops.
Reproducibility: All random seed, LLM version, full candidate text, and sample splits are stored.
Cost control: Estimate "number of candidates x evaluation batches x number of API calls" per iteration and fix the upper limit.
Common pitfalls (the paper points out)
dev over-training: selection with only fixed D_val -> production failure. → subsample/fold back validation.
LLM rating bias: "LLM-as-a-judge" preconceptions/style preferences. → multiple judges x aggregation.
"evil twins"/gibberish dividers: strings that are uninterpretable but work (reproducibility x safety risk).
Self-reflexive misguidance: erroneous error identification -> worse. → Examine the quality of negative examples and induction prompts.
Log probability requests (NLL/entropy) may not be possible with the black box API.
Cost explosion: candidate proliferation x evaluation multistage. → early stop, candidate castration, compressed FB.
Margins of Research (Next Steps)
Task-independent APO (task boundaries are blurred in actual operation)
Simultaneous optimization of the entire system/agent (SPRIG is the entry point, still heavy)
Multimodal APO (simultaneous optimization of text + image/voice)
Theoretical limits (AlignPro shows upper bounds, but lower bounds and general conditions are unorganized)
Minimum loop (pseudo code) that can be tried immediately
code:_
P ← SeedPrompts(hand | APE)
for t in 1..N:
C ← RewriteCandidates(P, LLM_feedback or GA or OPRO)
score(C) ← Eval(accuracy or reward or LLM-judge) on sampled D_val
P ← SelectTopK_or_UCB(C, score)
if no_gain ε for p rounds: break
return argmax_P Eval(P on full D_val)
On-site Tips (strips)
First, a "simple but strong" reference line (handwritten + small amount of few-shot + shaping instructions).
At least 2 LLM judges (different models/temperatures) + fixed criteria statement.
**Text optimal -> word substitution (COPLE)** at the end to pick up the slight increase.
**Consider MoE (MOP) or branching (AMPO)** if the application is broad.
For pipelines, DSPY/MIPRO optimizes by stage.
Safety/style is versatile and turns together (SOS/CRISPO style).
If necessary, we will create a **specific experimental design (D_val design, K/N, budget)** for your actual data (e.g., classification, summary, Q&A) and OPRO/[ProTeGi]/DSPY slapping prompts.

lines.text: Better to let LLM make the prompt.
[GPT5.icon]
Main rationale for "prompts should be generated by the LLM"
1. auto-generated prompts tend to be more accurate than human-made prompts

ICLR 2023's Automatic Prompt Engineer (APE), which only allows the LLMs themselves to create a large number of candidate prompts and sorts them by score, has been found to match or exceed human prompts in 19 out of 24 tasks. ([OpenReview https://openreview.net/forum?id=92gvk82DE-&utm_source=chatgpt.com])
2.[OPRO]: Turning LLM as an "optimizer" continuously improves prompts.

Google/DeepMind's OPRO iteratively optimizes by having LLM generate new directives while embedding performance and evaluation values into prompts; reports cases of up to +8 pts for GSM8K and up to +50 pts for BBH, outperforming human design (code also available). ([arXiv https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.03409?utm_source=chatgpt.com])
3. design framework ([DSPy]) demonstrated reproducibility and portability of "learned prompts

Stanford's DSPy is a "teleprompter" optimization that automatically adjusts prompts for each RAG and multi-hop QA module, reporting consistent improvement over handwritten Few-shot. The ability to "compile" prompt optimizations on a pipeline-by-pipeline basis is a practical advantage. ([OpenReview https://openreview.net/pdf?id=PFS4ffN9Yx&utm_source=chatgpt.com])
4. "LLM-written queries/virtual documents" are more successful in search and RAG

[HyDE] is a method of having LLMs write "provisional answers (pseudo-documents)" first, and then retrieving them by embedding them. Experimental results showed that it tends to be wider and more accurate than general retriever, and the improvement was reconfirmed by the Fact Verification Task 3 bench in the follow-up test in 2025. ([arXiv https://arxiv.org/pdf/2212.10496?utm_source=chatgpt.com])
5. even in image generation, it is easier to get better output if the LLM formats the prompts

Microsoft's [Promptist] improves the quality of T2I output by simply rewriting the user input to the "model's preferred representation" using LLMs (model release). It is more stable to have LLM compensate than to have a "person write a long spell". ([arXiv https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.09611?utm_source=chatgpt.com])
6. versatile, with many ways to optimize even with black box assumptions

Black-Box Prompt Optimization (BPO), RLPrompt, ProTeGi, GrIPS, and others that automatically search for and enhance prompts "outside" of LLMs and rewards report steady improvement. It also works in the field with no additional learning and API assumptions. ([arXiv https://arxiv.org/pdf/2311.04155?utm_source=chatgpt.com])
7. the advantages of auto-optimization are being sorted out even at the review level

The 2025 Systematic Survey emphasizes the ability of automatic optimization (APO) to absorb fluctuations in performance due to "apparent trivial differences" in prompts, and supports the motivation for practical implementation. ([arXiv https://arxiv.org/pdf/2502.16923?utm_source=chatgpt.com])
When does it work particularly well (guidelines for determining implementation)?
When you cannot/do not want to re-train the model (SaaS API use, cost constraints). ([arXiv https://arxiv.org/pdf/2311.04155?utm_source=chatgpt.com])
Tasks for which evaluation metrics can be provided (e.g., percentage of correct answers/click rate/manpower rating, etc.). ([arXiv https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.03409?utm_source=chatgpt.com])

Situations where prompts tend to be long-winded, such as search preprocessing (query expansion and virtual document generation) and multi-stage inference. ([arXiv https://arxiv.org/pdf/2212.10496?utm_source=chatgpt.com])
Preprocessing of generative systems (e.g. T2I/TTS) with strong representation dependence. ([arXiv https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.09611?utm_source=chatgpt.com])
Risks and coping (short)

Over-learning/metric gaming: danger of only fitting the development set -> OPRO also warned in section 5.4. Holdout verification & A/B required. ([arXiv https://arxiv.org/pdf/2309.03409?utm_source=chatgpt.com])

Increased cost: search is expensive -> control candidate generation with censoring criteria, sampling small-scale -> gradual expansion. ([arXiv https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.03409?utm_source=chatgpt.com])
Minimal implementation type (OPRO/DSPy style)
1. determine the indicators (percentage of correct answers/preference judgment).
2. have the LLM create a candidate (directive, few-shot example, style, etc.)
3. automatic evaluation → leave only the top (human or LLM review).
4. history embedded in prompts and regenerated (evolution/bandit/RL/teleprompter)
5. fixed and operated -> continuous monitoring (re-optimize with distribution changes). ([arXiv https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.03409?utm_source=chatgpt.com])
Is it in the OpenAI best practices?[nishio.icon]
[GPT5.icon]
Yes, the official OpenAI documentation specifies the "let LLM create/improve prompts" method as a recommended technique.

Prompt Generation Guide: explains how to "create good prompts/improve existing prompts from task descriptions" with metaprompts (also mentions Playground metaprompts). ([OpenAI Platform https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/prompt-generation?utm_source=chatgpt.com])

Cookbook: Meta-prompting: Defined as "a technique for generating and improving prompts using LLMs" and provides instructions with examples. ([OpenAI Cookbook https://cookbook.openai.com/examples/enhance_your_prompts_with_meta_prompting])

Cookbook: Prompt Migration Guide: specifies "Step 3: Critique prompt shortcomings to GPT-4.1" and "Step 4: Automatically generate revised system prompts" as steps. ([OpenAI Cookbook https://cookbook.openai.com/examples/prompt_migration_guide])

Cookbook: Evaluation Flywheel: Introduces a practical flow of turning automatic prompt optimization tools with data for evaluation + automatic scoring. ([OpenAI Cookbook https://cookbook.openai.com/examples/evaluation/building_resilient_prompts_using_an_evaluation_flywheel])

Help Center Best Practices: present a general statement to iteratively improve the prompts (i.e., consistent with the style of letting the model suggest improvements). ([OpenAI Help Center https://help.openai.com/en/articles/10032626-prompt-engineering-best-practices-for-chatgpt])
The **expression is not "should always" but is positioned as a **recommended practice (metaprompting/auto-optimization)**.

OPRO
[Large Language Models as Optimizers]
https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.03409

The linked paper is entitled "Large Language Models as Optimizers (OPRO). In short, it introduces a method of using LLMs themselves as "optimizers". ([arXiv https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.03409?utm_source=chatgpt.com])
main point

Idea: Describe the task to be optimized in natural language, and throw a meta-prompt to LLM with a history of past "solution→score" (candidate solutions and their evaluation values); LLM will look at the meta-prompt and suggest a number of next candidate solutions, evaluate them externally, add them to the history, and repeat. It works as a gradient-free black box optimization. ([ar5iv https://ar5iv.org/pdf/2309.03409])
Example of application:
1. toy example of a small linear regression/traveling salesman problem (TSP), confirming behavior that approaches a good solution by learning the direction of improvement from the history alone.

The main goal is prompt optimization. For example, in GSM8K/BBH, OPRO's automatically generated "directives" sometimes show better accuracy than the famous human prompts. ([ar5iv https://ar5iv.org/pdf/2309.03409])

Typical results: In GSM8K, "Take a deep breath and work on this problem step-by-step." (80.2%) found by OPRO is more accurate than "Let's think step by step." (71.8%) found by human. BBH also shows examples of significant improvement ("up to GSM8K+8pt, BBH +50pt" in the paper). ([ar5iv https://ar5iv.org/pdf/2309.03409])
Mechanism (design key)
What to put in [meta prompt]:
(a) Task description (objective function and constraints, a few input-output examples if prompt optimization)
(b) List of previous solutions and scores (in order of score)
→ LLM looks at historical patterns, extracts "good" features, and generates new candidates. ([ar5iv https://ar5iv.org/pdf/2309.03409])

Balancing search and utilization: multiple proposals are generated at each step for distributed search, and search (high temperature)/utilization (low temperature) is adjusted by temperature. Implementation guidelines for stabilization are also described. ([ar5iv https://ar5iv.org/pdf/2309.03409])
Separation of scorer and optimizer: often separate LLMs for score evaluation (e.g. PaLM2-L, text-bison) and LLMs to optimize (e.g. PaLM2-IT, GPT-3.5/4). ([ar5iv https://ar5iv.org/pdf/2309.03409])
Minimal reproduction procedure (with official implementation)

Official implementation: `google-deepmind/opro` (scripts for GSM8K/BBH, linear regression, TSP available). Example: `optimize_instructions.py` to specify optimizer (generation side) and scorer (scoring side) to turn. ([GitHub https://github.com/google-deepmind/opro])
Where to use it in practice / Caution
Usage: Good for problems where an evaluation function is available but no gradient can be obtained (UI wording optimization, prompt design, heuristic search).
Caution:
Beware of over-fitting to the evaluator ("hack" vocabulary that only works for evaluated LLMs) → Validate with a different model/separation.
Cost control (API costs increase with each step multiple proposal generation) and early termination criteria.
The longer the history, the more it is subject to context constraints, so it is necessary to retain only the top k, etc. ([ar5iv https://ar5iv.org/pdf/2309.03409])
summary

OPRO = A framework that uses LLM as a gradient-free optimizer in a "generate with history -> evaluate -> append" loop. Practical gains have been confirmed with prompt optimization and the code is publicly available. ([ar5iv https://ar5iv.org/pdf/2309.03409])
If necessary, we will also create a metaprompt template and cost optimization design on the spot for your data set other than GSM8K/BBH.

Laplacian regularization of Tikhonov type
[Laplacian regularization] of [Tikhonov] type
Just to the point, formula, intuition, implementation, in that order.
What are you doing (formulation)

On the graph (G=(V,E)) (nodes=comments, weights (w_{ij})), we seek to keep (Y) as much as possible while smoothing the existing label (Y_0\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times T}) (one-hot/probability) of the LLM. The objective function is
\min_{Y}\ \underbrace{\mu|Y-Y_0|F^2}{\text{fidelity to original label}}
\underbrace{\mathrm{Tr}(Y^\top L Y)}_{\text{Smoothness on graph (Dirichlet energy)}}
where (L=D-W) is the (un-normalized) graph Laplacian and (\mu>0) is the weight.
From slope=0
(\mu I + L),Y=\mu,Y_0
is the normal equation of Laplacian regularization of Tikhonov type. It can be solved independently for each column (class) (rows are nodes).
Effect: Close nodes have similar (Y) and (Y) does not deviate significantly from (Y_0) → Label denoising & boundary shaping occurs on high-dimensional graphs.
Intuition (two physics and probability)
Physical metaphor (spring net): each side is a spring, (\mathrm{Tr}(Y^\top L Y)=\sum_{(i,j)}w_{ij}|Y_i-Y_j|^2) is spring energy.
While loosening the spring, (\mu|Y-Y_0|^2) pulls back to the original label as an external force. The equilibrium point is the solution.
Probability metaphor (spread/restart): with row probability (S=D^{-1}W)
Y^*=(1-\alpha),(I-\alpha S)^{-1}Y_0,\quad \alpha=\tfrac{1}{1+\mu}
and is equivalent to the stationary solution of **Random Walk + Restart (RWR)**.
In other words, "the probability spreads to the neighborhood, but returns to the original label with a certain probability.
Which Laplacian to use?
L (non-normalized): May be vulnerable to density irregularities.
Normalized Laplacian:
(L_{\mathrm{rw}}=I-D^{-1}W) (recommended and easy to implement)
(L_{\mathrm{sym}}=I-D^{-1/2}WD^{-1/2}) (theoretically clean)
(L_{\mathrm{rw}}), the above RWR equivalence formula is straightforward. For cosine similarity, symmetrization is standard with L2-normalization → kNN → mutual kNN.
hyperparameter
(\mu) (or (\alpha=1/(1+\mu)):
(\mu\uparrow) → (Y) is faithful (diffuse weak) to (Y_0).
(\mu\downarrow) → Smoothing strong, lick the boundary.
First, we sweep (\mu\in[0.02,0.2]) to determine the index of **kNN label purity↑/precision↑**.
k (number of neighbors): 30± as a starting point. If density difference is large, stabilize with mutual kNN/variable neighborhood.
Mounting note
1. weight matrix: (w_{ij}=\max(\cos(x_i,x_j),0)^p)((p\in[1,3])) for weak edge suppression.
Linear equation: ((\mu I+L)) is symmetric positive definite → conjugate gradient method (PCG) + preprocessing (IC(0)/AMG) is fast.
Solve for the number of classes (T) columns with the same coefficient matrix (multi right hand side).
Output: Probability interpretation (normalization) of each row (Y_i), where `argmax` is the final label and `max` is the confidence level.
If all cases are labeled (Y_0) is one-hot or probability. This works as a **"label smoothing filter "**.
Relationship with other methods
Label Propagation (with clamps): only some nodes are strictly fixed ((\mu\to0) and boundary conditions).
The convergent solution of LGC: (Y_{t+1}=\alpha SY_t+(1-\alpha)Y_0) agrees with the above equation.
GFHF: corresponds to harmonic extension (absorption boundary).
→ This method is a **unified "smoothness + fidelity "** framework that includes them.
Where to use (in this case)
All cases have LLM labels → Put the whole (Y_0) to remove noise.
If a **lightweight classifier (logi-regression/SVM)** is then retrained with high confidence points, the decision boundary is even more stable.
The visualization is "just for show" with supervised UMAP (`target=y_hat`, `alpha=conf to opacity`).

To put it in a messy language.

In order to solve the problem that "it is difficult to be useful for decision-making and consensus-building even if diverse arguments are collected," which became apparent through the operation of IIDOBATA, we are collecting diverse positions on the same Statement (bluemo).

lines.text: AI dictatorships are better on average.
I take it as a given that "[AI Dictatorship] is [average] good," but I thought there was a discrepancy there first.
Governing by [AI smarter than the average human]" is naturally better than "governing by the average human" in terms of average performance.
But when you factor in factors other than "average," it's possible that human involvement in governance would be better.
For example, if you leave it to an AI, it will consistently score 80, but if you leave it to a human, the average score will be 70 and the [standard deviation] will be 10.
Then there's a non-negligible probability that human governance will do better than AI governance.
When it is possible for other countries to use a successful example from somewhere else as a reference, it is better to increase the variance even if it lowers the average.
There's also the question of how to measure the "performance" of governance.

bowling green
[Bowling Green]
Similar to [Shin Tokyo 2050 Broad Listening], a case study of [broad listening] using AI for long-term visioning.

Official article: [How one of the fastest-growing cities in Kentucky used AI to plan for the next 25 years | by Jigsaw | Jigsaw | Medium https://medium.com/jigsaw/how- one-of-the-fastest-growing-cities-in-kentucky-used-ai-to-plan-for-the-next-25-years-3b70c4fd1412]
relevance
[/blu3mo-public/Bowling Green's Comprehensive Planning with Polis].
[GPT5.icon]
Just a quick point 👇.
What article?

Case study of Bowling Green, Kentucky (population approx. 75,000, projected to double in 25 years), where citizen feedback was collected by [Polis] and summarized and categorized by Jigsaw's AI tool [Sensemaker] for the "BG2050" long-term plan (published 4/15/2025). ([Medium https://medium.com/jigsaw/how-one-of-the-fastest-growing-cities-in-kentucky-used-ai-to-plan-for-the-next-25-years-3b70c4fd 1412])
implementation method

A month-long online dialogue, "[What Could BG Be? Approximately 8,000 people participated, voting for and against thousands of unique proposals over 1 million times. Input is open-ended design. ([Medium https://medium.com/jigsaw/how-one-of-the-fastest-growing-cities-in-kentucky-used-ai-to-plan-for-the-next-25-years-3b70c4fd 1412])
Role of AI (Sensemaker)

Automatically clusters submissions into 12 topics and 72 subtopics to visualize support and polarization (mixed opinion). Generates reports in minutes, shortening analysis that would otherwise take days or weeks. ([Medium https://medium.com/jigsaw/how-one-of-the-fastest-growing-cities-in-kentucky-used-ai-to-plan-for-the-next-25-years-3b70c4fd 1412])
Major Findings

A surprisingly wide agreement was found with the majority (2,370) having an agreement rate of over 80%. In addition to transportation and roads, nightlife/entertainment, art and festivals, green space, and community pride emerged as priorities. ([Medium https://medium.com/jigsaw/how-one-of-the-fastest-growing-cities-in-kentucky-used-ai-to-plan-for-the-next-25-years-3b70c4fd 1412])

Differentiation of interest between K-12 and higher education (practical skills education vs. economic impact of college). ([Medium https://medium.com/jigsaw/how-one-of-the-fastest-growing-cities-in-kentucky-used-ai-to-plan-for-the-next-25-years-3b70c4fd 1412])

Local context + human review is essential (e.g., understanding the background of riverfront development). ([Medium https://medium.com/jigsaw/how-one-of-the-fastest-growing-cities-in-kentucky-used-ai-to-plan-for-the-next-25-years-3b70c4fd 1412])
Impact measurement (post-questionnaire)

Seventy percent of participants said that they felt more confident that their voices would be heard, and 83% said that they had a better understanding of different perspectives / better planning. Leaders rated the report as saving an average of 28 days of man-hours. ([Medium https://medium.com/jigsaw/how-one-of-the-fastest-growing-cities-in-kentucky-used-ai-to-plan-for-the-next-25-years-3b70c4fd 1412])
Scale Effects

Enables incorporation of almost 80 times the number of citizens into a plan originally considered by 100 leaders. Suggests lateral expansion to other cities as a prototype for large-scale, continuous consensus building. ([Medium https://medium.com/jigsaw/how-one-of-the-fastest-growing-cities-in-kentucky-used-ai-to-plan-for-the-next-25-years-3b70c4fd 1412])
Suggestion (if you want to put it into practice).
1. design questions broadly and freely, and collect a large number of evaluations (pros and cons)
2. quickly summarize, cluster, and map agreement and conflict with AI
3) Interpret with local knowledge and take measures from high-consensus areas, and dig deeper in polarized areas.

4. measuring psychological and administrative effects through post-event questionnaires - quantitatively demonstrating "a sense of having one's voice heard" and usefulness in decision-making (also effective in providing a budgetary basis)
